title: The Problem of Longitude
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: For centuries, sailors who lost sight of land could not say exactly where they were. Finding latitude, their position north or south of the equator, was relatively easy: a navigator measured the height of the sun at noon, or of the pole star at night, and consulted a table. Longitude, the position east or west, was a far harder problem. The Earth turns through fifteen degrees every hour, so a navigator who knew the time at his home port, and who could tell when it was noon where he was, could work out how far east or west he had travelled. The difficulty was knowing the time at home. The pendulum clocks of the period lost or gained minutes on a rolling ship, and changes in temperature and humidity made them still less reliable.

The cost of this ignorance was terrible. In 1707 a fleet of British warships returning from the Mediterranean misjudged its position in thick fog, and four ships were wrecked on the rocks of the Isles of Scilly with the loss of more than a thousand sailors. Public anger forced the government to act. In 1714 Parliament passed the Longitude Act, which offered a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds, a fortune at the time, to anyone who could find a way of determining longitude at sea to within half a degree.

Two approaches competed for the prize. The first was astronomical. Because the Moon moves across the sky against the background of the stars in a predictable way, a navigator could measure its position, compare it with printed tables, and so calculate the time at Greenwich. The method worked in principle, but the calculations were long and difficult, and they could take a sailor several hours. The second approach was to build a clock accurate enough to keep the time of the home port through a long voyage. Many leading scientists, including Isaac Newton, doubted that such a machine could ever be made, and most of them favoured the astronomical method.

The man who proved them wrong was John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from Yorkshire. Harrison understood that the problem lay in the mechanism's sensitivity to its surroundings, and he set about removing each cause of error in turn. He made parts of his clocks from a hard wood that needed no oil, and he combined strips of brass and steel in a way that cancelled out the effect of temperature on the pendulum. In 1730 he travelled to London with his designs, and his first sea clock was tested on a voyage to Lisbon in 1736. It performed well enough for him to receive money to continue.

Harrison's first three clocks were large and heavy, and he spent nearly thirty years improving them. His fourth machine, finished in 1759, was completely different: it looked like an oversized pocket watch, only about thirteen centimetres across. In 1761 it crossed the Atlantic to Jamaica, and on arrival it had lost just five seconds in eighty-one days, which was well within the standard that the prize required. Yet the Board of Longitude, the committee responsible for the award, refused to pay in full. It demanded further trials and insisted that Harrison hand over the watch and its designs so that copies could be made.

Some members of the Board were astronomers, and they had a natural preference for their own method. One of them, the Astronomer Royal, Nevil Maskelyne, was involved in judging the tests, and Harrison believed that he could not be impartial. After years of delay, Harrison, by then an old man, appealed to King George III. The king tested a later watch himself and found it excellent, and in 1773 Parliament awarded Harrison a large payment, though never the prize itself. In the writer's view, a man who had solved the problem so convincingly deserved to be rewarded far sooner.

The new instruments soon proved their worth. Captain James Cook took a copy of Harrison's fourth watch on his second voyage and described it in glowing terms, and within a few decades ships' chronometers had become cheap enough to be carried by most vessels. Navigators could at last fix their position with confidence, and voyages became shorter and safer. The idea that time and place are connected has not gone out of date: modern satellite navigation systems also work by comparing the precise time signals that reach a receiver from space.
